headline: 274 social-science claims retested. How much did the correlations shrink?
title: Investigating the replicability of the social and behavioural sciences
note: Of 274 positive claims from 164 papers in 54 journals, 151 (55.1%) yielded a significant result in the original direction. The paper-weighted estimate was 49.3%. For claims measured with Pearson’s r, the median fell from 0.25 to 0.10.

headline: 100 psychology studies repeated. How many still reached significance?
title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
note: The team repeated 100 studies from three psychology journals. Significant results went from 97% in the originals to 36% in the replications. Replication effects averaged about half the original magnitude.

headline: What happened when teams redid 21 experiments from Science and Nature?
title: Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015
note: Thirteen of 21 experiments yielded a significant result in the original direction. Replication effect sizes were about half the originals on average.

headline: 50 cancer biology experiments repeated. How much smaller were the effects?
title: Investigating the replicability of preclinical cancer biology
note: Researchers repeated 50 experiments from 23 papers. Of 97 originally positive effects assessable by five criteria, 39 (40%) met at least three. For originally positive effects overall, the median replication effect size was 85% smaller than the original median.

headline: How many experimental market findings held up in 166 new markets?
title: Do Experimental Asset Market Results Replicate? High-Powered Preregistered Replications of 17 Key Results
note: The team retested 17 results from four studies using 166 new markets with 1,544 participants. Three of the 14 originally significant results replicated, including findings about trading experience and cognitive skills.

headline: 18 economics lab experiments redone. Which way did the effects go?
title: Evaluating replicability of laboratory experiments in economics
note: Eleven of 18 lab experiments from the American Economic Review and Quarterly Journal of Economics produced a significant effect in the original direction. Replication effects averaged 66% of the original size.

headline: Many Labs 2 tested 28 findings in 36 countries and territories
title: Many Labs 2: Investigating Variation in Replicability Across Samples and Settings
venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
note: Across 125 samples with 15,305 participants, 15 of 28 findings produced same-direction effects at p < .05. For 21 of 28 findings, the replication effect was smaller than the original.

headline: Many Labs 3 asked whether the academic calendar changes replication outcomes
title: Many Labs 3: Evaluating participant pool quality across the academic semester via replication
note: The project retested 10 published effects across 20 university participant pools and an online sample. Three of 10 replicated at p < .05. The study found little evidence that semester timing changed the strength of the effects.

headline: Many Labs 5 rewrote 10 replication protocols. Did that restore the effects?
title: Many Labs 5: Testing Pre-Data-Collection Peer Review as an Intervention to Increase Replicability
venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
note: Teams retested 10 findings from the 2015 psychology project, selected because original authors had questioned the protocols. Two revised protocols reached p < .05, compared with zero using the earlier replication protocols. Across originals and replications, the combined median r was .07, versus .37 across the originals.

headline: What happened when 26 online experiments from PNAS were repeated?
title: Examining the replicability of online experiments selected by a decision market
note: Researchers repeated 26 of 41 eligible MTurk experiments, including 24 selected by a decision market. Fifty-four percent replicated by the significance criterion. Replication effects averaged 45% of the original estimates.

headline: 29 pandemic-era behavioral claims tested with independent data
title: Predicting the replicability of social and behavioural science claims in COVID-19 preprints
note: Of 29 claims selected from COVID-19 preprints, 11 of 16 replicated with newly collected data and 8 of 13 replicated with separate existing data, under the project’s success criterion.

headline: 56 biomedical experiments from Brazil repeated by independent labs
title: Estimating the replicability of Brazilian biomedical science
note: The project completed 143 replication attempts covering 56 experiments. For 17 of 39 experiments with multiple replications, the original estimate fell inside the replication meta-analysis’s 95% prediction interval. This is the reviewed preprint.

headline: What did 11 years of student-led replications find?
title: Eleven years of student replication projects provide evidence on the correlates of replicability in psychology
note: The project compiled 176 attempts. The mean judged success score was 49%. Of 136 replications with numerically comparable effects, 46% had an estimate inside the prediction interval based on the original result.

headline: Only 7 of 25 sports-science studies met all three replication criteria
title: Estimating the Replicability of Sports and Exercise Science Research
note: Teams repeated 25 studies from top-quartile sports-science journals. Only 7 (28%) met all three criteria: significance, the original direction, and compatible effect sizes. The other 18 missed at least one criterion.

headline: Only 2 of 10 influential sensory-marketing findings replicated
title: Evaluating replicability of ten influential research on sensory marketing
note: Preregistered online replications reached significance in the expected direction for 2 of 10 findings. All 10 replication estimates were smaller than the originals. The study also tested generalization to a different consumer population.

headline: 17 failed psychology replications got a second chance. Twelve failed again.
title: Estimating the Replicability of Psychology Experiments After an Initial Failure to Replicate
note: Researchers made fresh attempts on 17 previously unsuccessful replications. Five mostly or fully reproduced the original pattern by the project's ratings, with smaller effects. The other 12 were judged unsuccessful again. These projects were selected for prior failure.

headline: 18 frequently studied depression candidate genes revisited in large samples
title: No Support for Historical Candidate Gene or Candidate Gene-by-Interaction Hypotheses for Major Depression Across Multiple Large Samples
note: Across datasets totaling 621,214 individuals, the study found no clear support for the historical candidate-polymorphism effects or gene-by-environment interactions. The analysis tested 18 genes repeatedly studied in earlier depression research.

headline: 32 tests of published gene–intelligence links yielded one nominally significant result
title: Most Reported Genetic Associations With General Intelligence Are Probably False Positives
note: Researchers retested associations involving 12 specific variants across three independent longitudinal datasets. Only one of 32 tests across the datasets reached nominal significance.

headline: 14 leading schizophrenia candidate genes tested in an independent case–control sample
title: No Significant Association of 14 Candidate Genes With Schizophrenia in a Large European Ancestry Sample: Implications for Psychiatric Genetics
note: Researchers tested variants in 14 previously proposed candidate genes. Neither the gene-based tests nor the primary single-variant analyses produced associations that survived correction for multiple comparisons.

headline: Bayer compared published findings with in-house outcomes across 67 projects
title: Believe it or not: how much can we rely on published data on potential drug targets?
note: Bayer reported that the relevant literature fully agreed with its in-house findings in about 20–25% of 67 drug-target projects. Forty-seven projects were in oncology. This is an aggregate industry report with limited project-level disclosure.

headline: Amgen reported confirming 6 of 53 landmark preclinical cancer papers
title: Raise standards for preclinical cancer research
note: Amgen researchers reported confirming key findings in 6 of 53 papers their teams attempted to verify. This is an aggregate industry report. The commentary gives no study-by-study list of outcomes.
